scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: Twice a day, the sea rises up the beach and then pulls back. What moves an entire ocean?

scenes.name: moon
scenes.text: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth, and pulls slightly harder on the side facing it.

scenes.name: bulge
scenes.text: That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges, one facing the Moon, and one on the opposite side.

scenes.name: rotate
scenes.text: As Earth spins through these bulges, most coasts get two high tides and two low tides each day.

scenes.name: late
scenes.text: The Moon moves along its orbit, so tides arrive about fifty minutes later each day.

scenes.name: sun
scenes.text: The Sun pulls too. When Sun and Moon line up, we get extra big spring tides, and smaller neap tides when they don't.

scenes.name: coast
scenes.text: Coastline shape matters. Some bays funnel water into huge tides, others barely notice.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Moon pulls, Earth spins, oceans bulge. Follow for more on how things really work.
